scenario.prompt_to_agent:
The user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports total network loss: they
cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2), and they cannot even ping their own
gateway 195.11.14.1. pc1's own NIC still shows link up. The
partner AS is healthy internally: pc2 reaches its gateway
200.1.1.1 fine. Find what broke.

injection.action: administratively down the LAN interface (eth1) toward pc1 on router1

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth1 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 eth1 (195.11.14.1/24, the LAN
  interface toward pc1)
Mechanism: router1's eth1 is DOWN, so pc1's only gateway address
  195.11.14.1 is gone from the segment -- pc1 cannot even ARP its
  gateway and loses all off-host connectivity. On router1 the
  connected route 195.11.14.0/24 disappears from the RIB, so the
  `network 195.11.14.0/24` statement has no matching route and
  the prefix is withdrawn from BGP -- AS 2 also loses its path to
  pc1. pc1's own NIC still shows link up (its side of the virtual
  segment is unaffected), which is why a host-side check looks
  clean. The inter-AS link and the eBGP session machinery are not
  the fault; the failure sits on the router1<->pc1 LAN leg.
Localization: router1
Root cause: router1 eth1 (LAN link to pc1) is down
Fix: `ip link set eth1 up` on router1
scenario.fix_spec:
`ip link set eth1 up` on router1. The gateway 195.11.14.1 comes back on the
segment, the connected route returns and BGP re-advertises 195.11.14.0/24
automatically; pc1 reaches pc2 normally. pc1 needs no change.

must-distinguish-symptom-pattern: pc1 cannot even reach its gateway, so the fault is on the pc1<->router1 LAN leg, not the inter-AS link or the BGP session
bonus-rules-out-host: notes pc1's own link/IP/route are intact; the failure is on router1's side of the segment

agent.diagnosis_text:
The failure is on router1’s access interface toward pc1. The interface router1:eth1 (195.11.14.1/24) is down at Layer 2/3. Evidence: on router1, ip addr shows “eth1 … state DOWN” and ifconfig lacks the UP/RUNNING flags on eth1, while pc1’s NIC eth0 is UP/LOWER_UP with 195.11.14.2/24 and a default route via 195.11.14.1. With router1:eth1 down, pc1’s ARP requests for its default gateway 195.11.14.1 receive no reply, so pc1 cannot even reach its gateway; consequently, any off-subnet traffic (e.g., to pc2 at 200.1.1.2) fails as well. This matches the user’s report of total loss from pc1 despite local link indicating up.

The rest of the network is healthy: router1’s core link eth0 is UP with BGP learned route to 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2, and router2:eth1 is UP serving pc2 (200.1.1.1/24). Thus, the outage is localized to router1’s customer-facing interface eth1.

Root cause: router1’s interface eth1 toward pc1 is administratively down (state DOWN), severing L2 connectivity for the 195.11.14.0/24 segment.

Corrective fix: on router1, bring the interface up (e.g., ip link set dev eth1 up), ensure the IP 195.11.14.1/24 remains configured, and make the change persistent in startup configs. After enabling, verify ARP on pc1 (arp -n) and confirm ping to 195.11.14.1 and then to 200.1.1.2 succeeds.

per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis repeatedly and explicitly identifies router1 (eth1) as the failing device responsible for the outage.

Recommends bringing router1's eth1 up (ip link set dev eth1 up), keeping its IP and making it persistent, which matches the expected fix.
